topic: The Collision-Pi Connection: How Bouncing Blocks Calculate the Circle Constant
target_audience: High school students and undergraduate students interested in the intersection of physics and mathematics.

sections.title: The Setup: A Simple Counting Game
lecture_lines: Meet our setup: a frictionless floor and a wall.
We have a small block and a massive block.
The larger block slides toward the smaller one.
They bounce between each other and the wall.
Our goal: count every single collision that occurs.
animations: Draw a white (#FFFFFF) floor and a grey (#808080) wall.
Place a green (#00FF00) 'Mouse' block and orange (#FFA500) 'Elephant'.
Slide the orange Elephant block towards the green Mouse block.
Animate the Mouse block bouncing between the wall and Elephant.
Highlight every collision point with a small white (#FFFFFF) circle.

sections.title: The Pattern: A Mysterious Sequence
lecture_lines: Equal masses result in exactly three total collisions.
Increase the large mass by one hundred times.
Now we count thirty-one collisions between the blocks.
At ten thousand times the mass, it's three-hundred-fourteen.
The digits of Pi appear as mass ratios grow.
animations: Show ratio 1:1 with a counter hitting '3' collisions.
Update ratio to 1:100 and counter hitting '31' collisions.
Update ratio to 1:10,000 and counter hitting '314' collisions.
Highlight the digits 3, 1, 4 in yellow (#FFFF00).
Display a large cyan (#00FFFF) Pi symbol next to results.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Conservation Laws
lecture_lines: Kinetic energy is conserved in these elastic collisions.
Momentum also remains conserved during each block impact.
These laws strictly limit the velocities of both blocks.
animations: Write 1/2 mv² + 1/2 MV² = E in white (#FFFFFF).
Show a green (#00FF00) bar representing the constant energy budget.
Shift energy between blocks while keeping the total bar height.

sections.title: Mapping to Geometry: The Velocity Space
lecture_lines: Let's plot both velocities on a two-dimensional grid.
Energy conservation forces the velocities onto an ellipse.
Each collision moves our state to a new point.
animations: Draw axes v (#00FF00) and V (#FFA500) on a 2D plane.
Plot a white (#FFFFFF) ellipse representing the conservation constraint.
Move a white (#FFFFFF) point along the ellipse during collisions.

sections.title: The 'Circle' Trick: Scaling the Axes
lecture_lines: We can scale the axes to simplify the math.
This transformation turns the ellipse into a perfect circle.
Now, physics behaves like simple, beautiful circular geometry.
animations: Show the white (#FFFFFF) energy ellipse on the velocity axes.
Mathematically squash the horizontal axis to form a circle.
Highlight the new perfect cyan (#00FFFF) circle in the center.

sections.title: Collisions as Arc Segments
lecture_lines: Every collision is a jump along the circle's arc.
The jump distance depends on the specific mass ratio.
We count how many jumps fit in the circle.
This total count matches the digits of Pi perfectly.
Collisions map directly to the circle's total circumference.
animations: Show a cyan (#00FFFF) circle with a starting velocity point.
Animate a yellow (#FFFF00) line bouncing as an arc segment.
Label each bounce point with an incrementing collision number.
Visualize the jump length determined by the mass ratio.
Count jumps until the point leaves the 'collision' region.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Universal Language
lecture_lines: Linear block collisions hide a secret circular nature.
Conservation laws naturally link physics to the constant Pi.
Mathematics provides a universal bridge across different worlds.
animations: Zoom out to show blocks and the circle together.
Trace the digits of Pi around the circle in white (#FFFFFF).
Display the text 'Physics is Geometry' in the center.
